items.title: Section: The Wearing Effort of Benefiting Others, and the Plain Tedium of Ordinary Daily Tasks

items.zh: 利他處苦者，謂諸菩薩修十一種利有情業，如前應知。由彼所生種種憂苦，菩薩一切皆能忍受，不由此緣精進懈廢，如是名為菩薩忍受利他處苦。所作處苦者，謂諸菩薩或是出家，便有營為衣鉢等業；或是在家，便有無倒商估、營農、仕王等業。由此發生種種勤苦，菩薩一切皆能忍受，不由此緣精進懈廢，如是名為菩薩忍受所作處苦。
items.en: Suffering tied to benefiting others: bodhisattvas who cultivate the eleven kinds of work benefiting sentient beings, as should be understood from what was already described earlier, fully endure whatever worry and hardship arises from this work, never letting their diligence in practice slacken because of it — this is called a bodhisattva's enduring suffering tied to benefiting others. Suffering tied to ordinary daily tasks: bodhisattvas who are ordained have the work of maintaining robes, bowls, and the like; those who are lay have the work of honest trade, farming, or government service. Bodhisattvas who fully endure whatever exertion arises from these various tasks, never letting their diligence in practice slacken because of it, are said to endure suffering tied to ordinary daily tasks in this way.

items.title: Section: The Benefit of Enduring Suffering Well — Patience Calmly Enduring Suffering Closes

items.zh: 又諸菩薩雖觸眾苦，而於無上正等菩提，未正勤修能正勤修，已正勤修能無退轉，常勤修習，無變異意、無雜染心。是名菩薩安受眾苦忍。
items.en: Furthermore, though bodhisattvas encounter all this suffering, with respect to supreme awakening: one who has not yet begun genuinely diligent practice becomes able to begin it; one who has already begun genuinely diligent practice becomes able to never turn back from it — constantly practising diligently, the mind never wavering, never contaminated by affliction. This is called a bodhisattva's patience calmly enduring suffering.

items.title: Section: The Patience of Resolute Understanding — Eight Grounds for Genuine Conviction, and a Vagrant Bodhisattva's Test of His Own Patience

items.zh: 云何菩薩法思勝解忍？謂諸菩薩於一切法能正思擇。由善觀察勝覺慧故，能於八種生勝解處善安勝解。云何八種生勝解處？一、三寶功德處，二、真實義處，三、諸佛菩薩大神力處，四、因處，五、果處，六、應得義處，七、自於彼義得方便處，八、一切所知、所應行處。又此勝解由二因緣，於彼諸處能善安立。一、長時串習故；二、證善淨智故。是名菩薩法思勝解忍。
items.en: What is a bodhisattva's patience of resolute understanding grounded in reflection on the dharma? Bodhisattvas who are able to correctly reflect on and discern all phenomena, through genuinely skilful examination by superior wisdom, are able to establish settled, resolute understanding well within eight specific grounds. What are these eight grounds for resolute understanding? First, the genuine qualities of the three jewels; second, ultimate truth; third, the buddhas' and bodhisattvas' great and inconceivable spiritual power; fourth, cause; fifth, fruit; sixth, the goal genuinely worth attaining; seventh, the very means by which that goal is attained; eighth, everything genuinely worth knowing and genuinely worth practising. This resolute understanding, moreover, becomes genuinely well established within these grounds through two causes: first, sustained habituation over a long period of time; second, the realisation of genuinely pure wisdom. This is called a bodhisattva's patience of resolute understanding grounded in reflection on the dharma.

items.zh: 如是菩薩依此二品一切忍故，當知廣開難行忍等諸相差別。

items.title: Section: The Patience of Difficult Practice — Tolerating Harm From Those Weaker, Subordinate, or Lower in Station

items.zh: 云何菩薩難行忍？當知此忍略有三種。謂諸菩薩，能於羸劣諸有情所，忍彼所作不饒益事。是名第一難行忍。若諸菩薩居尊貴位，於自臣隷不饒益事堪能忍受。是名第二難行忍。若諸菩薩，於其種姓卑賤有情，所作增上不饒益事堪能忍受。是名第三難行忍。
items.en: What is a bodhisattva's patience of difficult practice? One should know this patience is, in brief, of three kinds. Bodhisattvas who are able to endure harmful acts committed by beings genuinely weaker than themselves — this is called the first patience of difficult practice. Bodhisattvas who, occupying a position of high honour, are able to endure harmful acts committed by their own subordinates — this is called the second patience of difficult practice. Bodhisattvas who are able to endure serious harmful acts committed by beings of low social standing — this is called the third patience of difficult practice.

items.title: Section: Comprehensive-Gateway Patience — Tolerant of Everyone at Every Degree of Severity; and the Five Virtuous-Person Marks of Patience

items.zh: 云何菩薩一切門忍？當知此忍略有四種。謂諸菩薩於親所作不饒益事，於怨所作不饒益事，於中所作不饒益事，悉能堪忍；及於彼三劣等勝品不饒益事皆能忍受。云何菩薩善士忍？當知此忍略有五種。謂諸菩薩，先於其忍見諸勝利。謂能堪忍補特伽羅，於當來世無多怨敵、無多乖離、有多喜樂、臨終無悔、於身壞後當生善趣天世界中。見勝利已，自能堪忍，勸他行忍，讚忍功德，見能行忍補特伽羅慰意慶喜。
items.en: What is a bodhisattva's comprehensive-gateway patience? One should know this patience is, in brief, of four kinds. Bodhisattvas are able to fully endure harmful acts committed by a friend, by an enemy, and by someone neither friend nor enemy — and are able to endure all such acts whether mild, moderate, or severe in degree. What is a bodhisattva's virtuous-person patience? One should know this patience is, in brief, of five kinds. Bodhisattvas first see patience's genuine benefits: one able to endure finds, in lives to come, few enemies, little estrangement from others, abundant genuine joy, no regret at the moment of death, and, after this body has perished, rebirth in a favourable realm among the heavens. Having seen these benefits, bodhisattvas are themselves able to endure, encourage others to practise patience, praise patience's genuine benefits, and, seeing others genuinely able to practise patience, offer them comfort and genuine, shared joy.

items.title: Section: Comprehensive-Kind Patience Opens — Six Different Roots From Which Genuine Patience Can Grow

items.zh: 云何菩薩一切種忍？當知此忍，六種、七種，總十三種。云何六種？謂諸菩薩，了知不忍非愛異熟，由怖畏故，勤修行忍。於諸有情有哀憐心、有悲愍心、有親愛心，由親善故，勤修行忍。於其無上正等菩提猛利欲樂，為圓滿忍波羅蜜多，由是因緣，勤修行忍。如世尊說：夫出家者，具忍辱力。由是因緣，不應出家受具足戒而行不忍。由法受故，勤修行忍。種姓具足，先串習忍，於今現在安住自性，故能修忍。知一切法遠離有情，唯見諸法無戲論性，諦察法故，能修行忍。
items.en: What are the six kinds? Bodhisattvas who clearly understand that intolerance ripens into an unwelcome karmic result, and diligently cultivate patience out of fear of that result. Bodhisattvas who hold genuine compassion, genuine sympathy, and genuine affection towards beings, and diligently cultivate patience out of this warm affection. Bodhisattvas with intense, genuine longing for supreme awakening, who diligently cultivate patience precisely in order to fulfil the perfection of patience. As the World-Honoured One taught: "One who has truly left the household life possesses the very power of patience" — bodhisattvas who, understanding that it would be improper to receive full ordination and yet fail to practise patience, diligently cultivate it precisely because they have formally accepted the discipline that requires it. Bodhisattvas whose own spiritual lineage is already complete, who habituated themselves to patience in past lives, and who now, in the present, abide in this as their own innate nature, and so are able to cultivate patience. Bodhisattvas who understand that all phenomena are free of any fixed being at all, seeing only that all phenomena are free of conceptual elaboration, and who, through this genuine investigation into the nature of phenomena, are able to cultivate patience.

items.title: Section: Seven More — Patience Covering Every Severity, Every Being, Every Place, Every Time, and All Three Karmic Doors

items.zh: 云何七種？謂於一切不饒益忍，從一切忍。一切處忍，謂於屏處及大眾前皆能修忍。一切時忍，謂晝初分，若晝中分，若晝後分，若夜，若日，若去來今，若病不病，若臥，若起，常能修忍。由身行忍，不捶打故。由語行忍，不出一切非愛言故。由意行忍，不憤發故，不持污濁惡意樂故。
items.en: What are the seven kinds? Patience towards every kind of harmful act, regardless of its severity. Patience extended towards every kind of being, regardless of relationship. Patience in every setting, meaning bodhisattvas are able to practise patience equally whether hidden from view or standing before a large assembly. Patience at every time, meaning bodhisattvas are constantly able to practise patience — in the day's early period, its middle period, or its later period; at night; during the day; in past, future, or present; whether ill or well; whether lying down or rising. Patience expressed through the body, meaning never striking or beating another. Patience expressed through speech, meaning never uttering any hurtful word. Patience expressed through the mind, meaning never becoming inwardly enraged, and never harbouring a defiled, turbid intention.

blocks.text: The remaining sources of suffering, the third kind of patience, and the other aspects of patience.

The tiring work of benefiting beings, and ordinary tasks: "if ordained, providing robes and bowls; if lay, honest trade, farming, government service". Master Cháng Bǎi: in the world one must work at something.

Through bearing suffering, "one who has not begun genuine practice becomes able to begin it; one who has begun never turns back". Venerable Miào Jìng: two points of non-regression: the stage of forbearance and the path of seeing.
The patience of conviction towards the eight foundations (Day 337): "able to reflect on and discern all phenomena". Venerable Miào Jìng: 勝 is powerful; 解 is one's wisdom.

Enduring harm "from beings weaker than oneself, from one's own subordinates when in high position, and from those of low birth", when retaliation would be easy. Venerable Miào Jìng: lacking bodily strength, lacking mental strength.
Enduring harm from those of inferior, equal, or superior standing; of every degree. A patient person in future lives has "few enemies, few estrangements, much joy, no regret at death".

Patience from fear of intolerance's result; from compassion; and so on. Patience towards every severity, every being, "whether hidden from view or before others", at every time of day, in body, speech, and mind. Master Cháng Bǎi quotes: "Patience is the foremost path."

quiz.q: In suffering tied to daily tasks, what work does the treatise assign to lay bodhisattvas?
quiz.why: "If ordained, there is the work of providing robes and bowls; if lay, honest trade, farming, government service, and the like." Venerable Miào Jìng: "non-inverted" means lawful; "serving the king" means working in government.

quiz.q: Though encountering all this suffering, what results for the bodhisattva regarding awakening?
options: those not yet diligent become diligent, those diligent never turn back — mind unwavering and undefiled
quiz.why: "One who has not yet begun genuinely diligent practice becomes able to begin it; one who has already begun becomes able to never turn back from it." Master Cháng Bǎi: those already practising diligently do not regress because they endure suffering.

quiz.q: On "never turning back," at which stages does Venerable Miào Jìng say non-regression occurs?
options: two points: at the acceptance stage, and further at the path of seeing
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: there are two points of non-regression — reaching the acceptance stage, and going further to the path of seeing. Master Cháng Bǎi: bodhisattvas at the inner-ordinary acceptance stage and above no longer regress.

quiz.q: How do the two lectures explain "shèng jiě" (resolute understanding) in this patience?
options: Miào Jìng: "shèng" is strength, "jiě" is wisdom — decisive only with cultivated wisdom; Cháng Bǎi: reflecting on dharma needs resolute understanding to accept it — the highest patience
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "shèng" means powerful, "jiě" is your wisdom. Master Cháng Bǎi: reflecting on the dharma requires resolute understanding in order to accept it — this is the highest degree of patience.

quiz.q: What are the three kinds of difficult patience?
options: enduring harm from those weaker, from one's own subordinates, and from those of low birth
quiz.why: Enduring harm from beings weaker than oneself, from one's own subordinates when in high position, and from those of low birth. Master Cháng Bǎi: usually the strong bully the weak; this patience is very hard — the first difficult patience.

quiz.q: The first mark of the good person's patience is "seeing its benefits." Which benefits are listed?
options: few enemies, few estrangements, much joy, no regret at death, rebirth in a good realm
quiz.why: A patient person in future lives has "few enemies, few estrangements, much joy, no regret at death, and after death rebirth in a good realm." Master Cháng Bǎi: "I forgave them back then and didn't form bad karma with them, so I have no regrets."

quiz.q: On "practising patience because one has received the dharma," what precept-sūtra verse does Master Cháng Bǎi cite?
options: "Patience is the foremost path; the Buddha calls the unconditioned supreme; one who goes forth yet troubles others is no śramaṇa"
"Give rise to the mind without abiding"
"All conditioned things are like a dream"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi quotes: "Patience is the foremost path; the Buddha calls the unconditioned supreme; one who goes forth yet troubles others is not called a śramaṇa." Venerable Miào Jìng: "dharma" here means the discipline — accepting it is patience.
